title: Risk, amplified
description: Borrowing, beta, and both sides of the trade.

questions.prompt: What is the return on your own $100?
questions.context: You invest $100 of your own money and borrow $100 at zero interest for one period. Your $200 investment falls by 10%. Repay the $100 loan. Ignore taxes, fees, and margin calls.
questions.explanation: You end with $80 of equity. Losing $20 on your own $100 is a −20% return.
questions.detail: The investment falls from $200 to $180. After repaying $100, you have $80. Your equity return is \((80-100)/100=-20\%\). Debt does not absorb this loss in the stated example; the change in asset value is borne by your smaller equity stake.
questions.misconception: −10% is the asset return. The question asks for the return on your own money after repaying debt.

source.section: What Drives Beta? The 3 Core Economic Factors

questions.prompt: Now the same $200 investment rises by 10%. What happens to your $100 equity?
questions.context: Again, you borrowed $100 at zero interest. Ignore taxes, fees, and margin calls.

options.text: It becomes $120: a 20% gain, just as losses were amplified.
It becomes $110: debt only magnifies losses.
It becomes $140: both the asset and the loan earn 10%.
It becomes $120, so borrowing removes investment risk.

questions.explanation: $220 of assets minus $100 of debt leaves $120. Leverage amplifies gains and losses.
questions.detail: The asset gain is $20, all of which accrues to the initial $100 equity stake after the fixed debt repayment. That is a 20% equity return. A higher levered return in a good state is not evidence of stock-picking skill or free additional return: the downside exposure increased too.
questions.misconception: The lender is owed a fixed $100 in this example; the loan does not automatically grow with the risky investment.

source.section: What Drives Beta? The 3 Core Economic Factors; Paying for Alpha, Getting Levered Beta

pairs.right: Tends to move against the market.

questions.explanation: Beta describes sensitivity to market movements, not total risk or guaranteed returns.
questions.detail: Beta is the slope relating an asset’s returns to market returns. Larger positive beta means greater positive market sensitivity; negative beta means an opposing tendency. Company-specific shocks still matter for realized returns, so these are statistical relationships rather than exact daily rules.
questions.misconception: A beta of 0.5 does not mean half the market’s total volatility; the stock can have substantial idiosyncratic risk.

source.section: The Sensitivity Metric: What is Beta?

questions.prompt: A stock with beta 2 must rise exactly 2% on every day the market rises 1%.
questions.explanation: False. Beta is a statistical sensitivity, not an exact daily multiplier.
questions.detail: In a market model, a stock’s return includes a market-related component and a firm-specific component. Beta 2 describes the slope of the market relationship. Company news and other residual variation can move the stock away from the fitted relationship on any given day.
questions.misconception: A regression slope describes a tendency across observations; it is not a promise about any one observation.

source.section: The Sensitivity Metric: What is Beta?

questions.prompt: In a market model, a portfolio holds 80% in the market and 20% in an asset with beta −0.5. Compared with putting that 20% in cash (beta 0), what changes?

options.text: A positive return is guaranteed in every recession.

questions.detail: With cash, portfolio beta is 0.8. Replacing that cash with a negative-beta asset lowers market sensitivity to 0.7. The new asset can also introduce firm-specific risk, so lower beta does not establish lower total volatility, nor does it guarantee protection in every realized downturn.
questions.misconception: Negative beta can reduce market exposure without eliminating every source of uncertainty.
